cards.title: Hideo Tomioka
cards.sub: 2012 · Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Japan
cards.prompt: A blind percentage cannot see intent. So what is the only kind of exemption a switch can actually honour mid-disaster — and what did Japan do with it afterwards?
cards.answer: A pre-registered allowlist: emergency priority calls, decided long before the event. Afterwards Japan considered widening that list and deferred it to a review of network design capacity; call length limits stayed an open question.
cards.body: Deputy Director of the Telecommunications Policy Division at Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. On 16 March 2012 he set out the study group's conclusions in an English-language MIC presentation. Extending the emergency-priority-call list got "careful consideration based on a review of network design capacity". Call length limits and reduced-quality calls: "Issue for future study".

cards.title: The 80 percent restriction
cards.prompt: Same network, same days, from 11 March 2011: DoCoMo throttled one kind of traffic hard and left the other nearly alone. Which was which, and to what percentage each?
cards.answer: Voice was cut by up to 80 percent, 90 percent in certain areas, across Tōhoku and Kantō. Packet took only a temporary 30 percent cap in Miyagi, and none after that.
cards.body: "Communications traffic increased dramatically and it was difficult for calls to get through." Voice: maximum capacity restrictions of 80 percent, 90 percent in certain areas, across Tōhoku and Kantō. Packet: a temporary 30 percent cap in Miyagi, nothing after. The Disaster Message Board, opened nationwide on 17 March, carried about 3.79 million posts by 28 March.

cards.title: Restoration Status for Damage Caused by the Great East Japan Earthquake and Future Responses
cards.sub: 27 April 2011 · NTT Group joint news release
cards.prompt: The story gives one money number, DoCoMo's. What did the whole NTT Group book for the same fiscal year, and in which document would you look it up?
cards.answer: About 30.0 billion yen consolidated for the fiscal year ended 31 March 2011, excluding donations — in the NTT Group joint news release "Restoration Status for Damage Caused by the Great East Japan Earthquake and Future Responses", 27 April 2011.
cards.body: Joint release by NTT, NTT East, NTT DOCOMO and NTT Communications. Its financial-impact table is the citable one: DOCOMO about 6.0 billion yen for the year ended 31 March 2011, plus about 10.0 billion capex and 10.0 billion profit/loss from the next year on. Group consolidated: about 30.0 billion yen, excluding donations.

cards.title: Voice moved onto the packet tier
cards.prompt: Your phone today falls back to a data-borne message when a disaster jams voice. Trace it back: after 2011 Japan reached for a new product rather than a better throttle. Why could a throttle not have fixed this?
cards.answer: Because a percentage throttle cannot be told what a call is for — the only scope it has is a list drawn up beforehand. So the fix moved the traffic instead: emergency voice messages sent as files over the packet tier, which was throttled far less than voice. DoCoMo shipped it in March 2012.
cards.body: MIC convened the study group April to December 2011: academics plus carriers and industry bodies. Interim report July, final December. The congestion agenda: upgrade switch design capacity, keep emergency priority calls viable, expand means of communication other than voice. Carriers built emergency voice-message services over the packet network, with interface specifications for interconnection between carriers.
